title: Separating transient leakage exposure from endpoint cancellation in fast transmon single-qubit gates
authors: Haoran Yang, Fudong Liu, Weilong Wang, Yangyang Fei, Zheng Shan
abstract: Fast single-qubit gates on weakly anharmonic transmons are limited by leakage to noncomputational states, and standard mitigations such as DRAG (derivative removal by adiabatic gate) act on the leakage amplitude at the end of the gate. We show that this endpoint amplitude and the transient leakage exposure accumulated during the gate are two distinct control objectives that can be assigned to separate modules. The endpoint is a single sample of the drive spectrum, $|\tildeΛ(η)|^2$; the exposure is a band integral about $η$ and governs leakage under dephasing, and the spectral-null condition $\tildeΛ(η)=0$ constrains only the former. We realize this split in a path--endpoint separation pulse (PESP): a path-shaping pulse suppresses the exposure, and a two-tone endpoint-cancellation pulse cancels the residual amplitude. For a $10$ ns $R_{X}(π/2)$ gate at $η/2π=0.2$ GHz, in numerical simulations the path-shaping pulse reduces the dephasing exposure by ${\sim}21\%$ relative to cosine DRAG and the independently simulated Lindblad excess leakage by ${\sim}20\%$, consistent with $P_{\mathrm{excess}}^φ\simeqγ_φT\bar{P}_{A}^{\mathrm{deph}}$, whereas matched-budget endpoint-only and spectral-null controls leave it essentially unchanged. The residual endpoint floor splits exactly into a $|2\rangle$ back-action and a $|3\rangle$ cascade, which the two tones cancel one-to-one, driving the floor at the path-exposure knee from ${\sim}7\times10^{-7}$ to ${\sim}3\times10^{-8}$ without perturbing the path. By separating transient exposure from endpoint leakage, PESP turns leakage suppression in fast weakly anharmonic gates into a modular, interpretable control problem: dephasing-induced leakage and the coherent residual error are reduced by separate, individually verifiable modules.
summary: This paper introduces the Path–Endpoint Separation Pulse (PESP) technique to improve fast single-qubit gates on transmon qubits by treating transient leakage exposure and final state leakage as separate control problems. By applying a path-shaping pulse and an endpoint-cancellation pulse sequentially, the method achieves superior suppression of both dephasing-induced errors and coherent residual errors compared to standard techniques.
main_problem: Fast single-qubit gates on weakly anharmonic transmons are limited by leakage to noncomputational states, and standard mitigation techniques fail to address both transient exposure and endpoint errors independently.
main_result: The proposed Path–Endpoint Separation Pulse (PESP) successfully decouples these two control objectives, significantly reducing dephasing-induced leakage ($\sim 20\%$) and the residual endpoint floor ($7	imes10^{-7}$ to $3	imes10^{-8}$) independently.
method: The authors developed a staged pulse sequence combining a Path-Shaping Pulse (PSP) to suppress time-integrated exposure and an Endpoint-Cancellation Pulse (ECP) to null the final drive spectrum amplitude.
model_or_system: The system is based on transmon qubits modeled as weakly anharmonic oscillators, analyzed using a rotating-frame Kerr-oscillator truncation Hamiltonian. Leakage analysis involves tracking populations in higher energy levels ($|2angle, |3angle$).
key_observables: Endpoint Leakage ($|	ilde{\Lambda}(\eta)|^2$), Transient Leakage Exposure ($ ar{P}_A$), Dephasing-induced Excess Leakage ($P_{\phi}^{	ext{excess}}$), and Gate Fidelity ($F_{	ext{comp}}$).
important_parameters: Gate time (e.g., $10 	ext{ ns}$ for $R_X(\pi/2)$), anharmonicity ($\eta$), dephasing rate ($\gamma_\phi$), and the relative weights assigned to path vs. endpoint control.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that endpoint leakage and transient exposure are mathematically distinct control objectives, allowing for modular optimization; hardware limitations like ZOH sampling and LP filtering are also analyzed as constraints.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate pulse waveforms, spectral components, and leakage trajectories comparing PESP to standard DRAG. Tables quantify path reduction across parameter grids and detail the sensitivity of the final error floor to various hardware imperfections (amplitude mismatch, sampling rate).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the limitations of existing methods by distinguishing between endpoint and transient leakage sources. It then introduces the PESP protocol, detailing the PSP for path shaping and the ECP for endpoint cancellation. Finally, it validates the method through extensive numerical simulations testing robustness against noise, sampling artifacts, and parameter variations.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly modular and interpretable framework for quantum control in superconducting qubits, moving beyond monolithic optimization to address distinct physical error channels (coherent vs. incoherent).
